newsitem.title: UK: Softs outlook - Markets set to change recent pattern.
newsitem.headline: Softs outlook - Markets set to change recent pattern.

text.p: Soft commodity futures should ease their way out of last week's stiff trading patterns but New York's equivalent markets are expected to set the tone for much of the London sentiment, brokers said on Monday.

Cocoa looked ready to push away from its recent lows following strength in the US market although origin pressure was still hanging over the market, while coffee would start the week with a price reaction to Friday's stocks data, they said.

In cocoa, traders said market sentiment had turned less bearish on account of last week's fall in New York's net speculative long positions, implying possible short covering, and the passing of December's first tender day.
The London market had more downside exposure than New York where gains were more achievable.
"There is a lot of pressure from origins and the biggest factor is lack of industry interest," one trader said.
Brokers said London could still follow New York's technical rally but cautioned that positions would face heavy selling pressure about 20 stg above current levels.

The benchmark March contract was likely to hover in a range between 900 and 950 stg in the short term, but the fortunes of the New York market and the strength of sterling were expected to be determining factors for sentiment.
Cocoa arrivals in key grower Ivory Coast should continue to draw attention but assume more importance later in the season.
Initial movements in coffee should hinge on October stock data from the US Green Coffee Association (GCA), released after close of business on Friday.

"The (market) direction depends on how large the fall in green coffee stocks is," said one trader. Prices were expected to rise if the decline was more than 200,000 60-kg bags and fall if stocks dropped by less than 100,000 bags. The figure released late Friday was 351,000 bags.
Technical analysts said while London's key January contract was struggling to regain this month's highs, upside momentum was faltering and support was increasingly likely to be tested.
While the arabica situation is tight, supply of robustas is strong and keeping a lid on prices, leaving a wide differential.
"The differential suggests that there's not much of a supply problem in robustas," said another trader.
The centre of interest in world coffee markets last week was fixed on low US inventories, with exchange-certified stocks at an all-time low and small amounts of coffee pending grading.
The spot December arabica contract enters its first notice day on Tuesday and the tight physical supply could spark a squeeze if operators do not continue to liquidate positions.
"If there's no liquidation then they have to take delivery but there's no coffee around to satisfy demand and this could spark a squeeze," one trader said.
London's white sugar market was expected to consolidate around last week's lower levels and traders said a new dose of fundamental news was needed to spur activity.
But even with last week's spot expiry out of the way, activity was expected to remain generally subdued unless a new wave of demand was seen for quality whites.
"You might see a bit of consolidation around these levels," one broker said. "I think it's getting a little more neutral, people aren't that strongly-minded one way or the other."

Support for the front-month March contract was pegged at $300 per tonne but although the market was expected to remain weak in the short term, no sharp moves were on the cards unless the raws market made a sudden rally or decline, traders said.
